title: Disease data newsroom: make the numbers fair
subtitle: Research a source, compare denominators and publish an honest infographic
objective: Create an accurate disease-data infographic using a checked source, comparable population measures and a cautious conclusion.

sow.exactOutcome: Research disease statistics; create an infographic.
sow.alignment: Directly develops source research and an infographic from C 35. The offline source card supports source/date/denominator checking; constructed local data support original chart design. No official exam or epidemiological analysis claimed.

priorLearning: A fraction compares a part with a whole.
success: Record source, publication date, data year and what a figure measures.
Calculate cases per 1000 over the same period.
Create a chart with an accurate headline, source and limitation.

vocabulary.meaning: The number of recorded cases or events.
The population or total used as the bottom of a fraction.
Cases divided by the relevant population, multiplied by 1000, for a stated period.
The year the data describe; it may differ from publication year.
A concise visual explanation combining labelled data and words.
A pattern in which variables occur together; by itself it does not prove causation.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one selected response route; pen, ruler and calculator.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint. Optional word processor or spreadsheet.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page, one chosen response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the teacher answers before teaching. All numerical sample data in this lesson are constructed for learning.
Optional ICT: open a blank document/slide or spreadsheet. Columns A–C can contain town, cases and population; D2 formula =B2/C2*1000. Paper infographic works fully offline.

Preview the WHO source card sensitively: it concerns global deaths, with no personal discussion required. If unsuitable for a pupil, use the constructed town source card for the same source/measure audit.
safety: Paper and screen tasks; no biological sampling, cultures, medicine handling or personal health disclosures.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is included. Point, annotate, dictate or discuss quietly instead of writing or using a device.

misconceptions.claim: The largest case count means the highest population chance.
misconceptions.correction: Counts describe workload; a comparable population denominator is needed for frequency per person.

misconceptions.claim: A publication date is the year the measurements describe.
misconceptions.correction: Data year and publication date can differ.
misconceptions.check: Ask which year the WHO figure describes.

misconceptions.claim: A difference between towns proves its cause.
misconceptions.correction: It shows a descriptive difference; population makeup, detection and exposures may differ.
misconceptions.check: Ask what comparison has not been controlled.

misconceptions.claim: 75% means 75% of all people had the disease.
misconceptions.correction: The WHO denominator here is non-pandemic-related deaths globally, not all people or all infections.
misconceptions.check: Require pupils to finish “75% of what?”

access.supported: Same core scientific goal, with word bank, short prompts, read-aloud or pointing/dictation. Do not assign a route from diagnosis.
access.standard: Use the supplied evidence to explain and justify an independent scientific decision.
access.stretch: Optional challenge after secure core: evaluate a limitation and transfer the science. Higher-tier-only material, where present, is labelled explicitly.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer solo or partner work, a pass and quiet response. Allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task; no compulsory disclosure, performance or speed competition.

sources.title: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Biology 1 BI0 specification
sources.note: Used to check relevant Foundation curriculum content; this is teacher-authored practice, not an official assessment or complete unit. Checked 8 September 2026.

sources.title: WHO: Noncommunicable diseases
sources.note: Offline source card paraphrases the page dated 25 September 2025: at least 43 million NCD deaths in 2021 and 75% of non-pandemic-related deaths globally. Denominator and data year retained. Checked 8 September 2026.

sources.title: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Describing Epidemiologic Data
sources.note: Checked counts versus population comparisons, time/place/person context and chart labelling; lesson arithmetic and fictional town data are original. Checked 8 September 2026.

slides.title: A headline can be numerically true and misleading
body: “Town C has the most cases.”
Does that tell us which town has the largest proportion affected?
slides.notes: Display the raw-count claim. Let pupils predict; an answer about proportions requires denominators. The mission is an honest infographic, not identifying a real dangerous town.

slides.title: Read what the number means
body: R1. What does a denominator tell us?
R2. What labels does a bar chart need?
R3. Does a pattern alone prove a cause?
slides.notes: R1: relevant whole/population. R2: category labels, numerical axis with units, title, period and source. R3: no. Accept three key labels before adding the full source checklist.

slides.title: Research the source, not just the number
body: WHO page published 2025; data describe 2021.
The statistic measures deaths, not people infected.
Ask: who counted what, where and when?
slides.notes: Read the source card. Model: “I record WHO, the page title and URL, publication date, data year 2021, global scope and the death measure. I do not relabel 75% as a share of all people.” The page was checked on 8 September 2026; infer no current trend.

table.caption: Real WHO source; figures are estimates for 2021, not today’s school data.

slides.title: Work one fair population comparison
body: I divide by the relevant population first.
Then I express the result per 1000.
slides.notes: Model 12 ÷ 2000 = 0.006, then 0.006 × 1000 = 6. Keep new cases per 1000 people over 7 days in the final unit. This is a cumulative incidence proportion, commonly called a rate in school work; it is not cases per person-year.

visual.title: I keep the denominator in the calculation
visual.description: Worked constructed example:12 new cases among 2000 people during the same 7 days.12 divided by 2000 times 1000 equals 6 new cases per 1000 people over 7 days. This is a period proportion expressed per 1000, not a person-time incidence rate.

elements.text: I keep the denominator in the calculation

Same disease definition, same period,
comparable recording and population.

slides.title: A count answers one useful question
body: Counts show how many cases were recorded.
C has 30; B has 18.
Population sizes still differ.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “C recorded 12 more cases than B. That matters for workload, but C has six times B’s population. I cannot infer the higher proportion from the count.” Point to the zero baseline.

visual.title: Constructed town data: count of new cases
visual.description: Constructed same 7-day surveillance data: town A 24 new cases, B 18, C 30. A has 3000 people at risk, B 1000 and C 6000. Raw counts alone do not show the greatest proportion affected.

elements.text: Constructed town data: count of new cases

slides.title: Newsroom calculation desk
body: W1. Calculate each town’s cases per 1000.
Keep the same 7-day period in the label.
slides.notes: A: 24 ÷ 3000 × 1000 = 8; B = 18; C = 5. Ask pairs or a TA to verify one calculation. A spreadsheet is optional; the teacher guide supplies the exact arithmetic.

table.caption: Constructed data: same fictional infection, same 7 days and recording method.

slides.title: Switch the measure, test the headline
body: W2. Which town leads by count? Which leads per 1000?
Write the two different headlines.
slides.notes: C has the greatest count (30); B has the greatest value per 1000 (18). Use the controlled count/rate toggle or draw three bars on paper. Both claims can be true; neither proves a cause.

visual.title: Constructed town data: cases per 1000
visual.description: Same constructed 7-day data expressed per 1000 people at risk: A 8, B 18, C 5. B has the highest observed proportion, while C had the greatest count. This does not prove why the towns differ.

elements.text: Recorded new cases per 1000 people over 7 days

slides.title: Editors reject an unsupported cause
body: W3. “B’s water caused the difference.”
The table records no water exposure. Improve the claim.
slides.notes: Expected: B had the highest recorded new cases per 1000 during the period; the cause of the difference is not established. Suggest comparable testing and exposure information as additional research; pupils do not collect biological samples.
slides.reveal: B had the highest recorded cases per 1000 during these 7 days. The table does not establish why.

slides.title: Which caption is accurate?
body: Check measure, denominator and period.
slides.notes: B is correct. A confuses count and proportion. C confuses the denominator. D confuses publication and data dates.

options.text: C has the largest proportion because it has 30 cases.
B recorded 18 new cases per 1000 people in the same 7 days.
options.feedback: Yes:18 cases among 1000 people, with the period stated.

options.text: The WHO 75% means 75% of all people died.
options.feedback: The denominator is non-pandemic-related global deaths, not all people.

options.text: A page published 2025 must contain 2025 measurements.
options.feedback: The source card explicitly describes 2021 data.

slides.title: Make a useful infographic
body: Choose your response route.
Include a fair comparison and a clear source note.
slides.notes: Pupils use paper or a blank document. All sources and data are supplied; an internet connection is optional.

slides.title: Your one-page newsroom brief
body: Headline • labelled bars • one calculation.
Source/date • careful conclusion • one limitation.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Check the denominator before colour or layout. Accuracy and readability define a useful infographic. Each route supplies chart or response space.

slides.title: An editor checks the denominator
body: L1. Show your infographic to a partner, teacher or TA.
Audience asks: “Per 1000 of whom, during what period?”
slides.notes: Pupils use the audience question to revise an axis label or caption, or justify an accurate one. Quiet review counts. Avoid rewarding dramatic headlines over evidence.

slides.title: Publish only what the evidence supports
body: A count is not a population comparison.
A chart is not proof of a cause.
slides.notes: Model: “B has the highest recorded 7-day cases per 1000 in the constructed example.” Ask pupils to verify the caption retains the constructed-data label.

slides.title: Keep the denominator
body: E 1. Calculate 10 cases among 2000 per 1000.
E 2. Why give the data year?
E 3. Does the town table prove a cause?
slides.notes: E1: 5 per 1000 for the stated period. E2: publication year can differ from data year; data age affects interpretation. E3: no. Re-teach the fraction first if E1 is incorrect.

slides.title: Next useful step
body: Calculate • label • check a source • limit a claim.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Collect the infographic or annotated sketch; keep work private unless the pupil chooses to share.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Source and town data
pupilPages.intro: The WHO card is a real source summary. The town dataset is constructed for this lesson; keep them separate.

blocks.text: WHO source card (paraphrase): the page dated 25 September 2025 reports at least 43 million deaths from non-communicable diseases worldwide in 2021. These were 75% of global deaths unrelated to the pandemic. The measure is deaths, not infections. Source: WHO, Noncommunicable diseases; checked 8 September 2026.

Constructed Town Bulletin: three fictional towns; same infection definition, same 7-day period, no existing cases at start; count each new case once. Assume comparable recording. Age/exposure differences are not supplied.

blocks.prompt: W1. Calculate per 1000. W2. Compare count and proportion. W3. Improve the unsupported water-cause claim.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Make the fair comparison
pupilPages.intro: Formula: new cases ÷ people at risk ×1000. Use the shared page. Complete a paper infographic below.

blocks.prompt: S1. Calculate cases per 1000 for A, B and C. Show one calculation.
S2. Sketch three bars from zero, label towns and “new cases per 1000 people over 7 days”.
S3. Add a headline naming the town with the highest proportion. Add “constructed data” and one thing the table cannot prove.
S4. For the WHO source, record the data year and what the 75% denominator is. Alternatively audit the Town Bulletin’s period and population.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Create the infographic
pupilPages.intro: Use the space as a layout plan, then finish in a document/slide if available.

blocks.prompt: M1. Calculate each town’s cases per 1000, showing one method.
M2. Draw an infographic with a zero-based bar chart, labelled units/period and a factual headline.
M3. Add a constructed-data source note and a limitation that prevents a causal claim.
M4. Audit the WHO source: publisher, publication date, data year, measure and 75% denominator. Or audit the Town Bulletin’s equivalent details.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Audit an editor’s claims
pupilPages.intro: Optional data challenge. Same constructed 7-day period: town D records 6 new cases among 200 people; town E records 30 among 2000.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate D and E per 1000. Which has the higher count and which the higher observed proportion?
T2. In town D one extra recorded case would change its value by how much per 1000? Explain why a small count deserves caution.
T3. Can the original town data prove that a prevention programme caused B’s value? Give two missing pieces of evidence or study-design issues.
T4. Draft a two-sentence accurate infographic caption for D/E, including constructed-data status, period and a limit.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Numbers need context
pupilPages.intro: A clear label is part of the science.

blocks.prompt: E 1. Calculate 10 new cases among 2000 people per 1000 for one stated 7-day period.
E 2. Why distinguish the publication date from the data year?
E 3. Why can a town comparison not by itself prove a cause?
L1. What did your editor ask? Improve one label or explain why it was accurate.

answers.label: Retrieval
answers.answer: R1: the relevant whole or population. R2: title, category labels, numerical axis with units, period and source. R3: association alone does not prove a cause.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1: A = 8, B = 18, C = 5 new cases per 1000 people over 7 days. W2: C has the greatest count (30); B has the greatest observed period proportion (18 per 1000). W3: B has the highest recorded proportion; the table has no exposure data or controlled comparison establishing water as its cause.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: A is false: denominators change the comparison. B is correct: 18 per 1000 for the same 7 days. C is false: WHO uses non-pandemic-related global deaths as the denominator. D is false: publication date and data year can differ.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: A: 24 ÷ 3000 × 1000 = 8. B: 18 ÷ 1000 × 1000 = 18. C: 30 ÷ 6000 × 1000 = 5. These are period proportions per 1000, not person-time rates.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: Correct bars have heights 8, 18 and 5, a zero baseline, town labels A/B/C and units of new cases per 1000 people over 7 days. The headline names B as the highest observed proportion. A hand-drawn chart is valid.

answers.label: S3 / M3
answers.answer: Example: “B had the highest recorded 7-day cases per 1000 in this constructed example.” Source: constructed Town Bulletin. A suitable limit is that the table cannot establish cause; age and exposure may differ, and comparable recording is assumed.

answers.label: S4 / M4
answers.answer: WHO; publication date 25 September 2025; data year 2021; non-communicable disease deaths; 75% of non-pandemic-related global deaths. This is not 75% of all people. Town Bulletin alternative: teacher-constructed data, three fictional towns, the same 7 days, people at risk at the start. Its calendar publication date is not provided and must not be invented.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: D: 6 ÷ 200 × 1000 = 30. E: 30 ÷ 2000 × 1000 = 15. E has the higher count (30 versus 6); D has the higher observed proportion (30 versus 15 per 1000).

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: 1 ÷ 200 × 1000 = 5 per 1000. One extra recorded case changes D from 30 to 35 per 1000. Comparisons based on small counts can be sensitive to small changes and chance. Uncertainty is not quantified here.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: No. Useful missing evidence includes exposure or programme details, a baseline or comparison group, comparable case finding and population characteristics. Other factors may explain a difference. Advanced statistical tests are not required.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Example: “In these constructed 7-day data, D recorded 30 new cases per 1000 and E recorded 15, although E had more cases in total. The comparison describes an observed difference, not why it occurred.”

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1: 5 new cases per 1000 over 7 days. E2: data year identifies when the measurements apply. E3: the table supplies no experimental control or causal evidence. L1: accept a specific label, source or caption revision, or a justified confirmation. Secure core requires correct denominators, chart labels and source context. Re-teach by writing cases ÷ population before multiplying by 1000.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing plus explanation, annotations or writing as evidence.
A quiet review still has an audience: teacher or TA reads the pupil’s decision, asks one evidence question, and the pupil revises or confirms it.

School shorthand may call “cases per 1000 over 7 days” a rate. Strictly this constructed no-baseline-case example is a cumulative incidence proportion for a fixed period; it is not a person-time rate and not an age-standardised comparison.

Interactive We do toggles count and cases per 1000 using exactly A 24/3000, B 18/1000 and C 30/6000. Pupils predict the leading town, test the measure and explain the ranking change. Paper route W1–W3 recreates both comparisons.
The WHO source is used for source literacy, not merged into the fictional infection chart. Do not imply 2021 data describe current school risk.
